answer.observations: E0 (default) shows UDP delivered exactly its offered 300 Mbps, TCP delivered 299.885 Mbps, udp_loss_frac=0, drops_band0=0, drops_band1=0, tcp_retrans=0, and link_util=0.618051. The important unexplained result is that TCP always has data to send, yet it does not use the ~38% of the link that is idle; it receives almost the same rate as UDP even though UDP only needs 300 Mbps of a 1Gbps link. This could mean the scheduler is non-work-conserving and/or allocates by packet count rather than bytes, or it could mean TCP CUBIC/receive-buffer limits TCP to about 300 Mbps. A second unknown is the UDP-loss boundary: UDP demand is 300 Mbps, but the configured weightUdp may need to be larger than 0.30 if the scheduler is packet-count based.

answer.observations: E0/E1 show TcpCubic stays near 300 Mbps when weightUdp is 0.30-0.50, with zero UDP loss. E3 shows TcpBbr/TcpBic duration 30 and TcpBbr queuePkts 4 or 1000 are all within 0.1% of the TcpBbr duration-10/default-queue result. The series for r005 shows TcpBbr already at about 418.9 Mbps from t=2.1, cwnd 3,033,424 bytes, q_band1=0, no drops. The series for r006 shows TcpBic cwnd grows past 1 MB and q_band1=92, but throughput remains about 418.5 Mbps. The series for r007 shows TcpCubic cwnd reaches about 1,051,248 bytes and then throughput is about 418.6 Mbps. The main unexplained fact is why several different variants, queue lengths, and durations all plateau at about 418.9 Mbps: either a fixed receive-buffer/RTT bound is binding, or the scheduler's configured TCP share is binding, or both. The weightUdp knob has not yet been tested with TcpBbr, so it is not yet known whether increasing TCP's configured share can raise TCP above 418.9 Mbps or whether UDP loss remains acceptable at low weightUdp.

answer.observations: E4 closes the scheduler question: with TcpBbr, tcp_goodput_bps is 418901197 to the LAST DIGIT at weightUdp=0.30 (r012) and 0.20 (r013), identical to the default 0.50 (r005) and to queuePkts=4/1000 (r010,r011) at duration=10. So across weightUdp 0.2-0.5, queuePkts 4-1000 and duration 10-30 the plateau never moves (C7,C9,C10,C11,C12). UDP loss stays 0 everywhere (C13,C14). The only thing left unexplained is the cause of the ceiling itself. The number 418901197 matches the fixed 1 MB (2^20) receive buffer over the 20 ms minimum RTT: 1048576*8/0.02 = 419430400 bps, of which the measured value is 99.87% (it is also above the 10^6-byte value of 400 Mbps, confirming a 2^20 buffer and ~20 ms RTT). Two different variants (BBR 418.901, BIC 418.510, within tolerance) plateau at the same value, which points to the receiver's window rather than any variant's cwnd as the cap. No allowed knob changes the buffer or the link delay, so no setting can raise TCP above this ceiling; the remaining work is to record the verdicts, resolve the open whys, and report.

report.goal: Maximize tcp_goodput_bps subject to udp_loss_frac <= 0.01 (the brief's given goal).
report.limit: The fixed 1 MB (2^20) TCP receive buffer over the 20 ms minimum round-trip time (2x10 ms link delay) caps in-flight data at ~1,048,576 bytes, i.e. ~419.43 Mbps; the measured 418.90 Mbps is 99.9% of that ceiling. No knob touches these fixed resources: weightUdp down to 0.20 (TCP 80% share) leaves TCP unchanged (C11,C12), queuePkts 4-1000 leaves it unchanged (C9,C10), and duration 10->30 leaves it unchanged once plateaued (C7). BBR and BIC plateau at the same value (E2), showing the cap is the receiver window, not a variant's cwnd. Evidence: E2,E3,E4,C7,C9,C10,C11,C12.
report.explanation: TcpBbr fills the receive window within the first (unmeasured) second and then sits at the window/RTT ceiling, so tcp_goodput_bps is fixed at ~418.9 Mbps regardless of weightUdp, queuePkts or duration (C7,C9,C10,C11,C12). The only lever that moves the goal is the congestion-control variant: TcpCubic is still ramping at 10 s (299.9 Mbps) and only reaches 376.5 Mbps at 30 s, whereas TcpBbr/TcpBic reach the ceiling within 10 s (E2,C4,C5,C6). Because the ceiling is set by fixed settings and UDP loss stays 0 at every tested weightUdp (C13,C14), the no-effect knobs are left at their defaults and the variant is set to TcpBbr (TcpBic ties it within tolerance).
report.holds_when: Link delay 10 ms and 1 MB buffers as fixed; one backlogged TCP flow; UDP demand 300 Mbps so UDP+TCP (~719 Mbps) stay below the 1 Gbps link and the scheduler never saturates.
report.breaks_when: If the receive buffer or RTT were larger the ceiling would rise; if UDP demand rose enough that UDP+TCP exceed 1 Gbps, weightUdp would bind and the recommendation would change; a loss-based variant that holds a standing queue would inflate RTT and fall below the ceiling.

claims.text: TcpBbr delivers ~418.9 Mbps, ~40% above TcpCubic's 10 s value, with udp_loss_frac 0.
The 418.9 Mbps plateau is identical to the last digit across weightUdp 0.2/0.3/0.5 and queuePkts 4/100/1000 at duration 10.
The plateau equals the 1 MB receive buffer / 20 ms RTT ceiling (~419.43 Mbps); extra scheduler share, queue length and duration do not raise it.
udp_loss_frac stays 0 at weightUdp as low as 0.20 with TcpBbr, so the constraint holds at the default weight.
TcpBic ties TcpBbr at the plateau within tolerance, so the choice among fast-fill variants is not critical.

open_questions: Whether the untested variants (Vegas, NewReno, LinuxReno) reach the same plateau; they cannot exceed it by the receive-window argument but were not measured.
The exact source of the ~0.1% shortfall below 419.43 Mbps (residual queueing vs buffer not fully filled); a series() on a TcpBbr run would show cwnd vs in-flight bytes.
